title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for defining and operating SLOs and error budgets, performing capacity planning, running reliability initiatives, conducting incident reviews, configuring operational tooling, and authoring runbooks. The goal is to provide a single, consistent set of expectations and templates so teams can reliably maintain production availability and make data-driven decisions about tradeoffs (latency, cost, and quality).

Scope
- Applies to all public-facing inference services, internal control plane services, and tenant-facing Dedicated/Private control planes.
- Excludes ephemeral dev/test infra unless a service overlaps production traffic.

Key definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): measured signal about user-observable behavior (e.g., successful request rate, p99 latency for generate endpoint).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): target on an SLI over a rolling window (e.g., 99.95% availability monthly).
- Error budget: allowable SLO violation budget (1 - SLO) used to make risk-based decisions about releases and operations.
- Toil vs. reliability work: operational tasks < 30 minutes and repetitive are considered toil and should be automated; reliability initiatives are project work with measurable impact.

Owner and governance
- SRE is the curator of SLO standards and incident-review processes. Product and Platform owners own service-specific SLOs and runbooks.
- Quarterly SLO reviews are required for any service that carries >1% of production requests or supports paying customers.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO design principles
- Measure user-impacting signals: success rate, latency (p95/p99 for interactive APIs), correctness where applicable (e.g., embeddings similarity baseline).
- Prefer multiple SLIs for a single user journey (availability + latency + correctness).
- Keep SLOs simple and actionable; tie them to business impact.
- Use rolling windows appropriate to cadence: 30-day rolling window for availability, 7-day for latency regressions, 1-day for critical pipelines.

Minimum required SLOs per service
- Availability SLO: percentage of successful requests (2xx or accepted responses) over 30 days. Default: 99.95% for public inference endpoints.
- Latency SLO: p95 and p99 for request-to-first-token and request-to-last-token. Default: p95 <= 150ms TTF (simple models) / <= 400ms (longer models) depending on model family; p99 defined per-service during onboarding.
- Error budget burn policy: define thresholds for green/amber/red based on burn rate over 24h and 30d windows.

Example SLO table (required fields)
| SLI name | Measurement | SLO target | Window | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| generate.success_rate | 2xx or streamed tokens observed | 99.95% | 30d | service-owner@example.com |
| generate.p95_ttf | time to first token (ms) | 150ms | 7d | service-owner@example.com |
| embeddings.p99_latency | end-to-end latency (ms) | 400ms | 30d | embeddings-team@example.com |

Error budget policy and automation
- Error budget calculation: error_budget = 1 - SLO. Track remaining budget daily and projected burn.
- Burn thresholds and actions (example):
  - Green: burn <= 1x expected -> normal operations
  - Amber: burn between 1x-3x -> schedule reliability investigation within 48h; freeze risky releases if burn continues
  - Red: burn > 3x or < 24h remaining at current burn -> immediate release freeze; paged to SRE lead; emergency postmortem triggered if incident ongoing
- Integrations: dashboards must show burn rate, time-to-empty projection, and links to on-call rota and runbooks.

2) Capacity planning and forecasting

Capacity planning cadence
- Monthly capacity review for critical services; quarterly for lower-tier services.
- Triggered re-planning if 10% sustained growth in QPS or token consumption week-over-week for 2 consecutive weeks.

Inputs and signals
- Past 90-day traffic and token usage trends broken down by: route, model family, request size distribution, client, and region.
- Burst tolerance (seconds of concurrency) and cold-start characteristics for model variants.
- Service-level SLOs and latency headroom requirements.

Capacity runbook checklist
1. Collect telemetry: QPS, tokens/sec, tail latency, instance CPU/GPU utilization, pod/container OOM counts, queue lengths.
2. Apply demand projections using 95th-percentile growth scenarios and seasonal multipliers.
3. Map demand to hardware: model-specific throughput (tokens/sec per GPU), batching efficiency, and quantization profiles.
4. Validate headroom: ensure 20% spare capacity under 95th-percentile forecast for critical services.
5. Define autoscaling policies: target CPU/GPU utilization, request queue length thresholds, and backpressure knobs.
6. Schedule procurement or reserved capacity purchases 60-90 days prior to predicted shortfall for Dedicated pools.

Capacity planning table (example values)
| Metric | Current | 95th forecast (90d) | Required buffer | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| avg QPS | 2,500 | 3,200 | 20% | model batching improves throughput |
| peak tokens/sec | 120k | 160k | 20% | consider burst autoscaler |
| GPU count (N) | 120 | 160 | 20% | include scheduled maintenance margin |

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Classifying reliability work
- Tier 0 (Critical): fixes that restore SLOs or prevent data loss within 24h.
- Tier 1 (High): automation to reduce toil or prevent repeated incidents (2-8 week projects).
- Tier 2 (Medium): performance optimizations that reduce cost per token but do not affect SLOs (quarterly roadmap).

RICE-style prioritization inputs
- R: Risk reduction (estimated % SLO improvement)
- I: Impacted customer segments & revenue exposure
- C: Complexity (engineering effort)
- E: Effort (story points or weeks)

Reliability initiative template
- Title
- Owner
- Problem statement and measured impact
- Proposed solution and rollout plan (canary + metrics)
- Success criteria and validation plan
- Rollback criteria and runbook links

4) Incident review and postmortem standards

Incident lifecycle and timelines
- Triage: within 15 minutes of first page.
- Initial incident summary: published within 60 minutes to #incident-bridge with impact, services, and mitigation steps.
- Post-incident review: a blameless postmortem published within 72 hours for SEV2/SEV1 and within 7 days for SEV3.

Postmortem template (required fields)
1. Summary and impact (affected services/customers, downtime, error budget burn)
2. Timeline of events with timestamps
3. Root cause analysis (RCA) and contributing factors
4. Corrective actions (short-term mitigations) with owners and due dates
5. Preventative actions (engineering work) with owners and due dates
6. Lessons learned and follow-ups
7. Attachments: logs, dashboards, runbook links, change IDs

Blameless reviews and action tracking
- Postmortems are blameless; focus on systemic fixes.
- All corrective and preventative actions must be entered into the reliability tracker with an owner and due date. Progress reviewed in weekly SRE sync.

5) Operational tooling and observability requirements

Mandatory dashboards per service
- SLOs & error budget summary (30d, 7d, 24h views)
- Request volume and request size distribution
- Latency heatmaps (p50/p95/p99) and tail analysis
- Resource utilization (GPU/CPU/memory) across model variants and shards
- Recent deployments and rollout status

Alerting standards
- Alerts must be SLI-derived where possible (e.g., golden SLO alert: projected time-to-empty < 48h).
- Avoid low-signal alerts; aim for precision. Each alert must have: symptom, probable causes, runbook link, paging threshold, and documented on-call owner.
- Alert severity mapping: P0/P1 for SLO-threatening incidents; P2 for degraded non-SLO issues; P3 for informational/trends.

Tooling integrations and automation
- PagerDuty for paging and escalation.
- Slack channels prefixed with #incident- for incident comms.
- Ticketing integrations: create JIRA incident task automatically when a SEV2/SEV1 is declared.
- CI/CD: deployments must include automatic SLO smoke tests in canary windows and rollback automation if SLO burn increases > 2x baseline within a canary window.

Example alert metadata (JSON example to copy into alert definition)
```
{
  \"alert_name\": \"generate_slo_time_to_empty\",
  \"symptom\": \"Projected error budget exhaustion < 48h\",
  \"paging\": \"true\",
  \"severity\": \"P0\",
  \"runbook\": \"/eng-sre/runbooks/generate-service-high-error-burn\"
}
```

6) Runbook standards and templates

Runbook purpose and format
- Every paged alert must link to a runbook. Runbooks are living documents; update after every use. Authors must add a brief runbook review note within 7 days after using it.
- Runbook sections: Overview, Preconditions, Quick mitigation steps, Diagnosis steps, Recovery steps, Post-incident tasks, Owner and escalation path.

Runbook template (markdown-style)
- Title: Service X - <alert or symptom>
- Owner: Team / Oncall
- Pagerduty: Escalation policy link
- Preconditions: what must be true to use this runbook (e.g., service has healthy control plane)
- Quick mitigation (first 5 minutes): numbered steps to reduce customer impact immediately
- Diagnosis (next 20 minutes): list of targeted checks and commands
- Recovery: steps to fully restore service
- Post-incident: notify stakeholders, create postmortem, update runbook
- Last reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD

Example quick mitigation for high latency on generate endpoint
1. Switch routing to lower-latency fallback model variant: `redwood route set --service generate --variant small-latency --weight 100`
2. Enable additional batching window: `kubectl patch hpa generate -p '{\"spec\":{\"scaleTargetRef\":{\"name\":\"generate\"}}}'` (team-specific ops assist may be required)
3. Temporarily increase Dedicated burst pool for customer tiers: contact Capacity on-call.

Diagnosis commands (examples)
- Check SLO dashboard: link to /dashboards/generate-slo
- Query recent errors: `curl -s "${LOGGING_URL}/query?service=generate&since=15m"`
- Check GPU utilization: `kubectl top pods -n inference --containers`

Runbook lifecycle and ownership
- Authors: service owners create runbooks during onboarding. SRE reviews runbooks for completeness during quarterly audits.
- Review cadence: runbooks must be reviewed at least once per quarter for high-risk services and annually for lower-risk services.

7) On-call and escalation guidance

On-call roles
- Primary: first responder performing initial mitigation and diagnosis.
- Secondary: backup if primary needs escalation or additional permissions.
- SRE lead: coordinates cross-team mitigation and release freezes.
- Incident commander: appointed for SEV1 incidents to coordinate external comms and exec updates.

Escalation timings
- If primary not responding in 15 minutes, escalate to secondary.
- If incident not contained within 30 minutes and error budget burn remains > 2x baseline, escalate to SRE lead and product manager.

8) Metrics, reporting, and review cadence

Regular reports
- Weekly SRE dashboard snapshot to engineering execs with top incidents, SLO burn trends, and capacity headroom.
- Quarterly reliability review with completed and planned reliability initiatives; update roadmap accordingly.

KPIs to track
- Mean time to detect (MTTD)
- Mean time to mitigate (MTTM)
- Monthly SLO compliance percentage per service
- Number of postmortems completed on time

Appendices

A. Example SLO calculation pseudo-SQL
```
SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN status_code >= 200 AND status_code < 300 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS success_rate
FROM requests
WHERE service = 'generate' AND timestamp >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';
```

B. Example runbook link inventory (examples)
- /eng-sre/runbooks/generate-service-high-error-burn
- /eng-sre/runbooks/generate-high-latency-fallback
- /eng-sre/runbooks/gpu-oom-recovery

C. Frequently asked decisions
- When to lower SLOs: only after quantified customer impact analysis and exec approval. Lowering SLOs requires a migration plan and communication to customers if contractual.
- Emergency procurement: SRE and Finance must sign off for Dedicated capacity purchases > $50k.

Contact and escalation list
- SRE pager: #sre-pager (PagerDuty integration)
- Capacity on-call: capacity-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Incident channel template: #incident-<service>-<YYYYMMDD>
